preamble: Rounding of [i] to [y] adds lip rounding to a high front vowel and leaves tongue position unchanged. It is usually triggered by neighbouring labial or labialized consonants. The textbook case is the 'Rundung' of the transition from Middle High German to New High German. Short i in a closed syllable, usually next to a labial, became ü [ʏ] in a handful of words, e.g. MHG finf > fünf, wirde > Würde, and flistern > flüstern. This ran alongside the parallel rounding of e > ö (helle > Hölle, zwelf > zwölf). Old Norse shows an older labial rounding: Proto-Germanic *i became y before a following w (v-umlaut, part of u-umlaut), as in *singwaną > syngva 'to sing'.

examples.from: Middle High German finf/vinf (< Old High German fimf) 'five'
examples.note: Short i rounded to ü between the labials f and n+f.

examples.from: Middle High German wirde (< Old High German wirdī) 'worth, dignity'
examples.note: Rounding after labial w. The German Rundung reader lists this example next to finf > fünf.
Rounding after the labial cluster fl-. Compare Yiddish פֿליסטערן (flistern), which keeps the unrounded vowel.
Labial (v-)umlaut: i rounded to y before the following w.
Listed as the i > y (+w-mutation) example in the Old Norse sound-change table.
Rounding between labialized consonants; kvikr keeps the unrounded vowel.
